messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Threat → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Marilyn, a 76-year-old radiologist of North American background, came to treatment after months of feeling as if the world had narrowed to the space inside her own apartment. During her late twenties she had been a young doctor living with her husband in a city caught in war, and one afternoon the building near the clinic where she worked was struck while she was still inside. She remembered the sound first: a shock so violent that the walls seemed to fold in on themselves, followed by dust, screaming, and the frantic rush of people trying to find the stairs. Since then, what remained most vivid was not a neat story but flashes she could not easily put into words. Those flashes made her feel at risk of being pulled back under at any moment, and she learned to keep the television on, scroll through her phone, or stay busy late into the night so the memory would not have room to gather strength. When she tried to talk about it, she found herself stopping, ashamed by the way the memory seemed to break apart in her mind, as if she ought to be able to explain it yet could not. Even now, when she deliberately tried to remember, the details felt slippery and inaccessible, and that difficulty itself deepened her sense that something unbearable sat just out of reach.

In the months after that event, Marilyn began organizing her life around not having to feel much of anything. She had come to believe that if she allowed herself to go back toward the memory, even by accident, she would be overwhelmed by shame, grief, or terror that she might not be able to stop. So she kept herself busy in ways that dulled emotion rather than invited it, spending long hours on her phone, in games, or scrolling the internet late into the night. She also stopped making plans for the future; appointments, travel, and even family gatherings felt like invitations to be disappointed or frightened. At home, her husband noticed that she would sit rigidly in front of the television, present but absent, because it seemed safer to avoid anything that might stir either painful or pleasant feeling. Yet the more she pressed the memory away, the less orderly it became when it surfaced. A smell of dust in a parking garage or the crash of something dropped in a hallway could bring back fragments she could not string together, and with each failed attempt to recall it deliberately, her conviction grew that the event was too shameful and too dangerous to face directly.

That sense of danger had also begun to shape how she moved through the ordinary world. Marilyn constantly scanned her surroundings for signs of threat, a habit that emerged most strongly when she left her building or walked into the radiology department where she still worked part-time. She watched doors, crowds, and parked cars before she noticed anything else, and unfamiliar places became nearly impossible because she could not assess the risk quickly enough. When the sense of danger was strongest, the memory of the bombing became harder to keep at bay, arriving with a bodily jolt as if the present threat had dragged the old scene back into view. A stranger approaching her in a grocery store aisle or a new patient standing too close at work could make her body tighten before the person had even spoken. The more she watched for danger, the more vivid and ungraspable the memory of the bombing became, arriving as bodily alarm rather than words. She would catch sight of a tall man in a dark coat, or hear a sudden bang from construction near the hospital, and the old scene would flare up in broken images she still could not fully tell aloud. That return of fragments left her more convinced that threat was everywhere, and the shame of not being able to explain what she remembered made her even more guarded.

Over time, Marilyn’s avoidance fed that vigilance in a way she could feel but did not know how to stop. Because she spent so much energy shutting down feeling and burying herself in screens, she had fewer moments in which the memory could settle into a story; instead, it remained jagged and intrusive, surfacing as disjointed sensations that kept her on edge. The less she could make sense of it, the more she stayed alert, and the more she stayed alert, the harder it became to recall the event in any coherent way. At work, she found herself cutting interactions short and avoiding unfamiliar parts of the hospital, and outside work she declined invitations from friends because new places felt impossible to assess. Even her marriage had become quieter and more constrained, with her husband unsure how to draw her out without making her retreat further. What finally brought Marilyn to seek help was a recent afternoon when a stranger stepped toward her on the sidewalk outside the clinic and she froze so completely that she could not continue walking. She left the appointment with her heart pounding and spent the rest of the day on her phone, trying not to think. She came because she was frightened that her world would keep shrinking, and because she hoped, with some doubt, that she might someday be able to remember without shame and move through ordinary life without feeling hunted.
